## Description

Taylor Series is an infinite sum of monomial terms. Taylor series acts like a polynomial with infinite terms. The series about $x_0$ converges for $|x-x_0|<R$ and diverges for $|x-x_0|>R$, where the radius of convergence $R$ is the distance from $x_0$ to the nearest singularity of $f$ in the complex plane. Asymptotes and growth rate on the real line do not decide it. $\arctan(x)$ and $1/(1+x^2)$ are smooth on the whole real line but have singularities at $\pm i$, so $R=1$ about 0; $\tanh(x)$ has poles at $\pm i\pi/2$, so $R=\pi/2$ about 0; $\log(x)$ about 1 has $R=1$ because of the singularity at $x=0$. Functions with no singularities, such as $\exp(x)$, $\sin(x)$, $e^{-x^2/2}$, $J_0(x)$ and the normal CDF, have $R=\infty$, whether or not they have horizontal asymptotes. The normal CDF (M18 below) has two horizontal asymptotes like $\tanh(x)$, and its order-10 polynomial pulls away from it beyond about $|x|=2$, but only because order 10 is too low: at $x=3$ the order-10 value is 2.0006 and the order-40 value is within $2\times10^{-7}$ of the true 0.99865.


Maclaurin and Taylor polynomials approximate a smooth function locally by truncating a power series. For center $x_0$, the degree-$n$ Taylor polynomial is

$$
T_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(x_0)}{k!}(x-x_0)^k.
$$

The Maclaurin polynomial is the special case $x_0=0$. Near singularities or non-smooth points, series may converge locally but fail globally.

A strong understanding of the Taylor series helps understand many numerical methods. Taylor series is often used in numerical methods to describe "the order of accuracy" or "order of convergence" of a particular numerical method. For instance, in numerical integration, a composite rule that integrates the constant and linear Taylor terms exactly, but not the quadratic term, is second-order accurate; the trapezoidal rule is an example.

A Taylor series is a special case of a power series. A related series is the Laurent series, which also allows negative powers of $(x-x_0)$. Padé approximant is very similar to a truncated Taylor series but is instead a ratio of two polynomials. Laurent series and Padé approximant may be discussed on other Numerical Methods pages.

## Video Animations

This section keeps some video animations I created before generated the GIFs.  They have a different aesthetic than the GIFs. The videos are generated by a MATLAB script:

[taylor_series_animation_code.m](taylor_series_animation_code.m)

### Exponential Cases, $exp(x)$ about 0 and 1

The Taylor series of $exp(x)$ about 0 has an infinite radius of convergence. Higher and higher-order Taylor series truncations converge more and more to $exp(x)$. $exp(x)$ about 1 is similar to $exp(x)$ about 0, except that the expansion point is 1.

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/hYLjC8gmXw0?si=DUFpW92jHjn-6sBQ >}}

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/27Ew6aE95YA?si=rj3TlEaEyetJg5bj >}}

### Sine Cases, $sin(x)$ about 0 and 0.5

Sine has no singularities in the complex plane, so its Taylor series converges for every $x$; the radius of convergence is infinite.

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/JM6h67hYZVU?si=rJfF8rm9iPh6IRSQ >}}

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/ZQeUI9CG_AU?si=IlQxkN1IDDVCgXA >}}

### Hyperbolic Tangent Cases, $tanh(x)$ about 0 and 0.5

Tanh has two horizontal asymptotes, but what limits the radius of convergence is its poles at $\pm i\pi/2$: the radius is $\pi/2\approx1.571$ about 0 and $\sqrt{0.25+\pi^2/4}\approx1.648$ about 0.5.

{{< video https://youtu.be/iuPJbubsJvA?si=EavU02OHSEzYK9GD >}}

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/ryRv-xhdQLs?si=qpfC4NvbhTbMvkWT >}}

### Inverse Tangent Cases, $arctan(x)$ about 0 and 0.5

arctan also has two horizontal asymptotes; its radius of convergence is limited by its singularities at $\pm i$: 1 about 0 and $\sqrt{1.25}\approx1.118$ about 0.5.

{{< video https://youtu.be/Xup7ESoOM68?si=r--FSOPR1FdW2eg4 >}}

{{< video https://youtu.be/H4zeDK8bf7M?si=p4s2V0i-ojrbQU6d >}}

### Rational and Singular Cases, $1/x$ about 0.5 and $1/(x-1)$ about 0.75

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/2GPi45LTiFU?si=Fn_GNEf_Bj0t61sJ >}}

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/fNKgR_sQwHM?si=6xe7H4mfj2Ob4Nj3 >}}

### Non-Smooth Case, $sqrt(abs(x))*sign(x)$ about 0.5

This function is built from abs, which is continuous but has a corner at x=0, and sign, which jumps at x=0; the composite itself is continuous. This function often is used by engineers to simulate lump parameter fluid flow. This function is a poor choice because the sqrt gives it an infinite derivative at x=0, so the Taylor series about 0.5 has radius 0.5. The Taylor series cannot converge across x=0.

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/3EJLus4Y_JY?si=XoqOby2mjnws1sTS >}}

## Animations

Each animation steps through the Taylor polynomials one order per frame, one frame per second, showing the current order (blue) and, from order 1 on, the previous order (gray) over the target function (magenta); the red dot marks $(x_0, f(x_0))$. Parts of a polynomial outside the plotted $y$-range are drawn along the top or bottom edge.

All 31 GIFs on this page are generated by one Julia script:

[Julia source for all cases](series_animations_all.jl)
